questions.prompt: Which package provides the local AerSimulator backend used to run and debug circuits entirely on your own machine, with no cloud account required?
options: qiskit-aer
qiskit-ibm-runtime
qiskit-algorithms
qiskit-experiments
questions.explain: qiskit-aer provides AerSimulator, the standard local, high-performance simulator. qiskit-ibm-runtime is the client for IBM's cloud hardware, qiskit-algorithms holds algorithm building blocks like Grover and VQE (moved out of core qiskit as of Qiskit 1.0), and qiskit-experiments provides characterization tools like readout-error calibration.

questions.prompt: A teammate says, 'I ran my circuit in Qiskit and got an unexpected result, so the quantum computer must be broken.' Which of the following are legitimate things to check first, given that Qiskit is a software framework with both a local simulator and a real-hardware path?
options: Whether the circuit actually ran on AerSimulator (noiseless) versus real hardware (which has gate and readout noise)
Whether the circuit's logic (gates, qubit indices, measurement wiring) actually matches what was intended
Whether enough shots were used, given that any finite shot count produces statistical shot noise even on a perfect simulator
Whether the office Wi-Fi router needs to be restarted, since that is what actually determines a qubit's measurement outcome
questions.explain: Qiskit being a framework means 'unexpected result' almost always traces back to which backend was used (simulator vs. noisy hardware), a logic bug in the circuit itself, or ordinary shot noise — not a vague claim that hardware is broken. A qubit's measurement outcome has nothing to do with network connectivity.

questions.prompt: Fill in the missing method name: `QiskitRuntimeService.______(channel="ibm_quantum_platform", token="YOUR_API_TOKEN", overwrite=True)` is the call that stores your IBM Quantum credentials locally so you don't have to re-enter them every session.
questions.explain: QiskitRuntimeService.save_account(...) persists your channel, token, and instance information locally; later sessions can call QiskitRuntimeService() with no arguments and it picks up the stored credentials automatically.

questions.prompt: A Bell-state circuit (`qc.h(0); qc.cx(0,1)`) run at 1024 shots gives `{'00': 503, '11': 521, '01': 0, '10': 0}`. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two kinds of 'not a perfect number' in this result?
options: The 503-vs-521 gap on 00/11 is ordinary statistical shot noise around an exact 50/50 probability, while the exact 0 counts on 01/10 reflect a true zero amplitude in the state that would stay exactly zero on every rerun, not noise at all
Both the 503-vs-521 gap and the 0-vs-0 outcomes are examples of the same kind of statistical shot noise, and both would change if you reran the circuit with a different seed
The 0 counts on 01/10 indicate a bug in the circuit, since a real Bell state should show small nonzero counts there
The 503-vs-521 gap indicates a hardware error, since a noiseless simulator should always produce an exact 512/512 split
questions.explain: The Bell state (|00>+|11>)/√2 has exactly zero amplitude on 01 and 10 — that zero is structural and reruns will not change it. The 503/521 split on 00/11 is the expected statistical variation from sampling a true 50/50 distribution a finite number of times, and it would look slightly different with a different random seed.

questions.prompt: Starting from |0>, `qc.h(0)` gives the exact statevector [0.7071068+0j, 0.7071068+0j], and `qc.rx(math.pi/2, 0)` gives [0.7071068+0j, 0-0.7071068j]. Which statements about these two circuits are true?
options: Both give measurement probabilities P(0)=0.5 and P(1)=0.5
The two statevectors are identical, so the two circuits prepare exactly the same quantum state
RX introduces a relative phase on the |1> amplitude (an imaginary component) that H does not
Because both give the same measurement probabilities, there is no way any future circuit step could ever behave differently depending on which of the two gates was used
questions.explain: Both states give identical measurement statistics (0.5/0.5) because probability depends on amplitude magnitude squared, but the states are not identical — RX(π/2) leaves an imaginary relative phase (−i on the |1> amplitude) that H does not produce. That phase difference is invisible to a direct measurement right here, but it is real and can affect the outcome of later gates applied to the qubit (e.g. another rotation), which is exactly why 'same measurement probabilities' does not mean 'same state.'

questions.prompt: For `qc.rx(theta, 0)` applied to a qubit starting in |0>, the exact closed-form probability of measuring |1> is P(1) = ______ (in terms of theta).
questions.explain: This closed form matches the verified table in the course: θ=π/2 gives P(1)=0.5, θ=π gives P(1)=1.0 (a full bit-flip), and θ=2π/3 gives P(1)=0.75 — all consistent with sin²(θ/2).

questions.prompt: Given the circuit `qc = QuantumCircuit(3); qc.h(0); qc.cx(0,1); qc.cx(1,2)`, which outcomes are structurally possible when you measure all three qubits, and with what exact probability?
options: Only `000` and `111`, each with exact probability 0.5
All 8 three-bit outcomes, each with exact probability 0.125
Only `000` and `100`, each with exact probability 0.5
Only `111`, with exact probability 1.0
questions.explain: This is the 3-qubit GHZ recipe: H creates a superposition on qubit 0, then each CX propagates the entanglement outward one qubit at a time, producing the exact state (|000>+|111>)/√2 with zero amplitude on all 6 other basis states.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about measurement in Qiskit are true?
options: Measuring a qubit collapses its superposition irreversibly into one definite classical outcome
`qc.measure_all()` measures every qubit into a matching set of classical bits
You can measure a qubit, read the result, and then restore it to its prior superposition if you need to
A classical register (or classical bit count) is required to receive a measurement outcome
questions.explain: Measurement is a one-way, destructive operation — once a qubit's superposition collapses to a classical value, there is no way to recover the prior superposition. measure_all() is the convenience for measuring everything at once, and a classical register is exactly the classical memory a measurement outcome is written into.

questions.prompt: A noiseless AerSimulator run of the Bell-state circuit at shots=4096 gives 2021 counts for `00`, not the 2048 you'd get from exactly 0.5 × 4096. Since this simulator has zero hardware noise modeled, what is the only possible source of that 2021-vs-2048 gap?
options: Ordinary statistical shot noise from drawing a finite number of samples from the true 0.5 probability
Gate miscalibration on the simulated CX gate
Thermal decoherence (T1/T2 relaxation) during the simulated circuit's execution
A software bug in AerSimulator's measurement routine
questions.explain: With no noise model attached, AerSimulator reproduces the circuit's ideal logic exactly — the only remaining source of variation is sampling: each of the 4096 shots is an independent draw from the true 0.5/0.5 distribution, and a finite sample practically never lands on the exact expected count.

questions.prompt: The standard error of an empirical measurement frequency over N shots, for a true outcome probability p, is SE = ______.
questions.explain: This is the standard error of a binomial proportion. It predicts, for example, SE≈0.0156 at N=1024 for p=0.5 — consistent with the roughly 1-percentage-point spreads seen in this course's seeded 1024-2048-shot Hadamard and Bell-state runs.

questions.prompt: A colleague doubles their shot count from 1024 to 2048, hoping to cut the standard error of a measured probability in half. Using SE ∝ 1/√N, which statements are correct?
options: Doubling N only reduces SE by a factor of 1/√2 (≈0.71), not by half
To actually halve SE, the shot count needs to be quadrupled (4x), not doubled
Shot noise disappears completely once you use more than about 2000 shots
The true underlying probability p changes as you take more shots
questions.explain: SE scales as 1/√N, so N needs to go up by a factor of 4 to cut SE in half (since √4=2). Doubling shots only shrinks SE by roughly 29%. Shot noise never disappears entirely at any finite N, and the true probability p is a fixed property of the circuit, not something that shifts with sample size.

questions.prompt: Under a noiseless Bell-state circuit, P(01) and P(10) are exactly 0. Add a 1% depolarizing error on the CX gate, and they become 0.0025 each, with a real sampled run showing small nonzero counts there. What does a nonzero measured count on `01`/`10` specifically tell you that a skewed `00`-vs-`11` split alone would not?
options: It signals an outcome that is classically impossible under the ideal circuit — a real sign of gate error, not just the ordinary statistical spread you'd see on an already-possible outcome like 00 or 11
It tells you the simulator ran out of memory partway through
It tells you the shot count was too low to get a meaningful result
It tells you the circuit was measured before the CX gate finished executing
questions.explain: 00 and 11 are both theoretically possible (each at 0.5), so any imbalance between them could plausibly be shot noise. 01 and 10 have exactly zero theoretical probability under the ideal circuit, so any nonzero count there can only come from a real error process — this is the key diagnostic difference the course builds toward in the capstone's validator.

questions.prompt: Which Qiskit visualization function maps a single-qubit state to a 3D arrow on the Bloch sphere?
options: plot_bloch_multivector
plot_histogram
plot_state_qsphere
plot_state_city
questions.explain: plot_bloch_multivector draws each qubit's state as a Bloch-sphere vector. plot_histogram visualizes measurement counts as bars, while plot_state_qsphere and plot_state_city visualize multi-qubit amplitude/phase structure that the single-qubit Bloch sphere cannot represent.

questions.prompt: Based on the verified Bloch-vector computations in this course, which of the following mappings are correct?
options: |0> (no gates) maps to Bloch vector (0, 0, 1)
H|0> (the |+> state) maps to Bloch vector (1, 0, 0)
X|0> (the |1> state) maps to Bloch vector (0, 0, -1)
RX(π/2)|0> maps to Bloch vector (0, 0, -1)
questions.explain: The first three are exactly the verified values: |0> sits at the north pole, H puts the state on the equator along +x, and X flips it to the south pole. RX(π/2)|0> actually lands at (0, -1, 0) on the equator along -y, not (0,0,-1) — RX rotates within the Y-Z plane, not toward the south pole.

questions.prompt: A colleague shows you a Bloch-sphere plot of one qubit from an entangled Bell pair, and the arrow sits at the center of the sphere instead of on its surface. What does that center position actually mean, and what should you use instead to properly visualize this state?
options: The individual qubit's reduced state is a mixed state (not a pure point on the sphere's surface), because entanglement means that qubit alone doesn't have a well-defined pure state — a Q-sphere of the full 2-qubit system is the right tool here
The plotting library made a rendering error and the plot should be regenerated
The qubit is in the exact |0> state, which happens to plot at the center for this particular library
The center position means the qubit was never actually measured
questions.explain: A Bloch sphere can only faithfully represent a pure single-qubit state. For a qubit that's part of an entangled pair, its individual (reduced) state is actually a mixed state with no definite Bloch vector of its own — the arrow collapsing toward the center is the correct visual signature of that, and the Q-sphere (which captures the full multi-qubit state, phase and all) is the appropriate tool instead.

questions.prompt: You have two real backends available: Backend A has more total qubits but a long queue and a coupling map that doesn't match your circuit's entangling pattern well. Backend B has exactly enough qubits, a short queue, and connectivity that matches your circuit closely. Which should you choose, and why?
options: Backend B — a short queue plus good native connectivity means less routing overhead (fewer inserted SWAP gates) and a faster turnaround, both of which usually matter more than having extra unused qubits
Backend A — more total qubits is always the dominant factor regardless of queue or connectivity
It makes no difference which backend you choose, since transpilation makes every backend behave identically
Backend A — a longer queue always means a backend has less real-world usage error accumulated
questions.explain: Backend selection in this course weighs qubit count, queue length, and connectivity together. Extra unused qubits don't help if the circuit you're running doesn't need them, while a poor coupling map forces the transpiler to insert extra SWAP gates (more noise, more depth) and a long queue delays your results — Backend B wins on the factors that actually matter for this circuit.

questions.prompt: A single Toffoli (CCX) gate, decomposed into a {CX, single-qubit gates} basis set, is standardly expanded into ______ CNOT gates (plus several single-qubit H/T/T† gates).
questions.explain: This is a well-known, documented circuit identity: the standard Toffoli decomposition uses 6 CNOT gates, which is exactly why a circuit written with only a handful of Toffolis can balloon in CNOT count once transpiled for a real backend's native basis gate set.

questions.prompt: You run a Bell-state circuit on (simulated) real hardware and get `{'00': 2005, '11': 2003, '01': 35, '10': 53}` out of 4096 shots. A teammate says this proves there's a bug in the circuit, since 01/10 should never appear. Which statements are correct?
options: The teammate is wrong — nonzero counts on 01/10 are the expected signature of real gate or readout error, not necessarily a circuit bug
From the counts alone, you cannot tell whether this specific error came from a gate acting right before measurement or from the readout hardware itself
This noise profile is consistent with a roughly 5% depolarizing-style error rate on the entangling gate, not with a logic error in how the circuit was written
This exact pattern can never occur on any correctly functioning real quantum device
questions.explain: Nonzero 01/10 counts are exactly what real hardware noise looks like on a circuit that should be noiseless in theory — it's the signature error-mitigation (Chapter 7) exists to address, not evidence of a logic bug. Counts alone can't separate gate error from readout error; that requires a separate characterization experiment.

questions.prompt: You have a small amount of real-hardware quota this month and three circuits: (1) one you've thoroughly debugged in simulation and are confident is correct, (2) one you're still actively finding bugs in, and (3) one you just want to see out of curiosity with no specific question in mind. How should you prioritize your scarce hardware quota?
options: Run circuit (1) first — validating an already-debugged circuit against real noise is the highest-value use of scarce quota; keep debugging (2) in free simulation until it's ready, and treat (3) as lowest priority
Run circuit (3) first, since curiosity-driven runs build the most intuition
Run circuit (2) first, since real hardware will help you find the remaining bugs faster than simulation would
Split the quota evenly across all three regardless of their readiness
questions.explain: Simulation is free and unlimited, so it's the right place to find and fix bugs — spending scarce real-hardware quota on a circuit still full of bugs or on idle curiosity wastes a limited resource. The highest-value use of quota is validating a circuit you already believe is correct against real-device noise.

questions.prompt: A colleague shows you `from qiskit.algorithms import QFT` and says it's from a tutorial they found. Which of the following are actually wrong with that import?
options: `qiskit.algorithms` was removed from the core qiskit package as of Qiskit 1.0 — algorithm building blocks like Grover and VQE now live in the separate `qiskit-algorithms` package
QFT specifically lives in `qiskit.circuit.library` (part of core qiskit), not in `qiskit-algorithms` at all
QFT does not exist anywhere in Qiskit and must be hand-built from controlled-phase gates every time
The import statement has correct capitalization and would work fine as written on any current Qiskit install
questions.explain: Two separate things are wrong: qiskit.algorithms no longer exists in core qiskit (moved to the standalone qiskit-algorithms package), and even within the current ecosystem, QFT specifically is a core qiskit.circuit.library class, not part of qiskit-algorithms at all. QFT does exist as a ready-made circuit — you don't have to hand-build it.

questions.prompt: For N=4 items with 1 marked item, exactly one Grover iteration gives probability 1.0 on the marked state. If you instead had N=16 items with 1 marked item, would one iteration still give exactly probability 1.0?
options: No — using (π/4)·√(N/M), N=16 and M=1 give an optimal iteration count around 3, not 1, and even the optimal integer iteration count only gets close to, not exactly, probability 1.0
Yes — the number of marked items (1) is what determines the exact-certainty result, regardless of N
No — Grover's algorithm only ever works for exactly N=4 search spaces
Yes — larger N always converges faster to exact certainty than smaller N
questions.explain: N=4, M=1 is a special case where (π/4)·√(N/M) works out to exactly 1 iteration with exact probability 1.0. For N=16, M=1, the formula gives roughly 3.14, so the nearest practical iteration count is 3 — and even that only reaches a probability close to, not exactly, 1.0, unlike the clean N=4 case.

questions.prompt: For a toy single-qubit Hamiltonian H = a·Z + b·X, the minimum achievable expectation value with any single-qubit state is exactly ______ (in terms of a and b).
questions.explain: Since Z and X anticommute and both square to the identity, (aZ+bX)² = (a²+b²)I, so the eigenvalues of aZ+bX are ±√(a²+b²). For the course's toy Hamiltonian H=0.5Z+0.3X, this gives the verified minimum -√(0.5²+0.3²) = -0.583095.

questions.prompt: Applying the 3-qubit QFT to |001> produces 8 output probabilities that are all exactly 0.125 — identical, in magnitude, to what a maximally mixed random state would show. What actually distinguishes the QFT's output from true randomness?
options: The QFT output has a specific, deterministic phase on each of the 8 amplitudes (encoding the original input), while true randomness has no such recoverable phase structure
Nothing distinguishes them — a flat probability distribution is a flat probability distribution regardless of how it was produced
The QFT output probabilities are only approximately 0.125, while true randomness would be exactly 0.125
The QFT output changes every time you run it, while true randomness is fixed
questions.explain: Measurement probabilities alone can't tell QFT output apart from a random state, since both look perfectly flat. What makes QFT output different — and genuinely useful in algorithms like phase estimation — is that the relative phases across the 8 terms are deterministic and encode the original input exactly; they're not discarded randomness.

questions.prompt: A noise model injects a true 2% bit-flip error probability on a qubit prepared in |0>, but a 1024-shot run on it comes back with an observed error rate of 2.34% instead of exactly 2.00%. Is this evidence the noise model is misconfigured?
options: No — this gap is ordinary statistical shot noise on top of the real injected 2% error; a finite sample of 1024 shots won't land on exactly 2.00% even with a perfectly correct noise model
Yes — any deviation from the injected error rate proves the noise model code has a bug
Yes — 2.34% vs 2.00% is too large a gap to ever be explained by shot noise
No — the noise model is working correctly, but only because 1024 shots happens to be an unusually noisy sample size
questions.explain: An injected 2% error rate is the true underlying probability; the observed 2.34% from 1024 shots is just one finite sample's draw from that distribution, subject to the same shot-noise statistics covered throughout this course. It is not evidence of a misconfigured noise model.

questions.prompt: Readout error mitigation uses `corrected = M⁻¹ · observed` to correct a known confusion/calibration matrix M. Which statements about this correction are true?
options: Applying M⁻¹ to the exact observed probabilities recovers the true distribution exactly
Applying M⁻¹ to sampled shot-count fractions only approximately recovers the truth, because shot noise on the raw counts can itself get amplified by the correction
Readout mitigation eliminates all statistical shot noise in addition to correcting the readout bias
Readout error mitigation corrects a systematic measurement bias that exists even when the underlying quantum state itself is prepared perfectly
questions.explain: The matrix correction is exact algebra when applied to exact probabilities, but real data comes from finite shot counts, so the correction only approximately recovers the truth and can slightly amplify statistical noise. It fixes a systematic measurement-hardware bias, not the underlying state — and it does not make statistical shot noise disappear.

questions.prompt: Given zero-noise-extrapolation measurements E(1) and E(2) taken at noise-scale factors λ=1 and λ=2, the linear extrapolation estimate for the ideal, zero-noise value E(0) is E(0) ≈ ______ (in terms of E(1) and E(2)).
questions.explain: This is the two-point linear extrapolation formula used in the course: with E(1)=0.72 and E(2)=0.64, 2(0.72)-0.64=0.80, exactly recovering the true ideal value in the course's deliberately linear teaching model.

questions.prompt: Using only the final measurement counts from a single circuit, can you tell whether an observed error came from a gate acting right before measurement or from the readout hardware itself?
options: No — the two are observationally indistinguishable from counts alone in a case like this; you need a separate characterization experiment (e.g. preparing known states and measuring them directly) to tell gate error apart from readout error
Yes — gate errors always produce exactly half the error rate of readout errors
Yes — readout errors only ever appear on even-numbered shots
No — this distinction is permanently unknowable even with additional experiments
questions.explain: A single circuit's counts give you a combined error signature; gate error and readout error on a single qubit measured right after the error can look identical in the counts. Separating them requires a dedicated characterization experiment (like the ones in qiskit-experiments) that isolates readout behavior from gate behavior.

questions.prompt: Walking through `qc.h(0); qc.cx(0,1); qc.cx(1,2)` on 3 qubits gate by gate, what are the two nonzero basis-state labels in the final state (Qiskit ket convention, read left-to-right as q2q1q0), and their amplitudes?
options: `000` and `111`, each with amplitude 0.7071068
`000` and `001`, each with amplitude 0.7071068
`000` and `011`, each with amplitude 0.7071068
`111` only, with amplitude 1.0
questions.explain: H(0) first produces {000, 001}, then CX(0,1) evolves that to {000, 011}, and finally CX(1,2) evolves it to the final GHZ state {000, 111} — each step propagating the entanglement one qubit further outward, ending with amplitude 0.7071068 on both 000 and 111 and exactly zero elsewhere.

questions.prompt: In the capstone's measurement-validation layer, which of the following statements are true?
options: A deviation within about 2 standard errors of a nonzero exact probability (like the GHZ case's ~1.99σ deviation on `000`) should generally not be flagged as a problem
Any nonzero count on an outcome where the exact theoretical probability is precisely zero should always be flagged, regardless of shot count
The standard-error formula SE=√(p(1−p)/N) can be applied unmodified when the exact probability p is exactly 0
Testing the validator against a known-answer case like the GHZ circuit is a meaningful way to check the tool is actually correct before trusting it on an unknown circuit
questions.explain: Ordinary statistical deviations within a couple of standard errors are expected and shouldn't be flagged, while any nonzero count where theory predicts an exact zero is a structural anomaly that should always be flagged — but the SE formula breaks down (gives SE=0) exactly at p=0 or p=1, which is why the validator needs a special case rather than applying the formula blindly. Validating against a known-answer case is exactly the right way to build confidence in a new tool.

questions.prompt: Extending the GHZ recipe to 4 qubits via `[('h',0), ('cx',0,1), ('cx',1,2), ('cx',2,3)]`, the final state has exactly two nonzero basis-state labels (in q3q2q1q0 ket order), each with amplitude 0.7071068. Those two labels are ______ and ______.
questions.explain: The same propagation logic applies one more step: H(0) then a chain of CX gates from each qubit to the next spreads the entanglement all the way to qubit 3, producing (|0000>+|1111>)/√2 — the general n-qubit GHZ recipe, with amplitude 0.7071068 on both all-zero and all-one labels and exactly zero everywhere else.
